header: IN THE LAHORE HIGH COURT, LAHORE
Order with signature of judge, and that of parties or counsel,
18.11.2026. Mr. Shahid Nazir Jarra, Advocate for petitioner.
body: Mr. Hamaad Iftikhar Syed, ADPP for State with Imtiaz SI. Nemo for respondent No.2.

Through this criminal revision under Sections 435 and 439, Cr.P.C., Muhammad Irfan (petitioner) has assailed the order dated 08.09.2025 (“impugned order”) passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Mandi Bahauddin, whereby the proceedings in the trial arising out of FIR No.1268 dated 02.09.2023, registered under Sections 302, 324, 337-A(i), 148 and 149, PPC, at Police Station Civil Lines, Mandi Bahauddin, were adjourned sine die on an application moved by respondent No.2/complainant, on the ground that the principal accused, namely Arsalan alias Chochi Shah, had absconded.

2. Briefly stated, the prosecution case, as reflected in the available record, is that respondent No.2 (Najam Shahzad) lodged the aforesaid FIR against the petitioner and others, alleging that the principal accused, Arsalan alias Chochi Shah, made a firearm attack upon Muhammad Arif (deceased), who subsequently succumbed to the injuries sustained in the occurrence. In the same occurrence, the role attributed to the petitioner is that he fired a shot at the injured, Rozina Farooq. After completion of the investigation, a report under Section 173, Cr.P.C. was submitted before the learned trial Court and proceedings commenced against the accused persons. During the course of the trial, the principal accused and certain other coaccused failed to appear before the Court and were reported to be proclaimed offenders. Consequently, on an application moved by learned counsel for respondent No.2, the learned trial Court, vide the impugned order dated 08.09.2025, adjourned the entire proceedings sine die till the arrest and production of the principal accused. Hence, the instant revision petition.

3. Learned counsel for the petitioner contends that the impugned order is contrary to the settled principles governing criminal trials and has been passed without lawful justification. It is argued that the petitioner is regularly appearing before the learned trial Court and cannot be deprived of his right to an expeditious conclusion of the criminal proceedings merely because another accused has absconded. He has, therefore, prayed that the impugned order be set aside and the learned trial Court be directed to proceed with the trial against the petitioner and the other available accused persons in accordance with law.

4. Conversely, the learned Law Officer supports the impugned order and submits that the principal accused has been specifically nominated in the FIR and that his role is material to the prosecution case. According to him, proceeding with the trial in his absence may result in inconsistent findings and cause prejudice to the prosecution.
5. Heard. Record perused.

6. The question requiring determination is whether the learned trial Court was legally justified in keeping the entire trial proceedings in abeyance for an indefinite period merely because the principal accused had absconded. The answer to this question lies in the scheme of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, particularly Sections 344 and 512 thereof, read with the constitutional guarantee of a fair trial and due process of law. Section 344, Cr.P.C. empowers a Court, where it is necessary or advisable to do so on account of the absence of a witness or any other reasonable cause, to postpone the commencement of, or adjourn, any inquiry or trial, by an order in writing stating the reasons therefor, from time to time, for such time as it considers reasonable. The expressions employed by the legislature, namely "from time to time" and "for such time as it considers reasonable", clearly indicate that the power of adjournment is to be exercised for a specified and reasonable period. The provision does not confer upon a Court of Sessions an unrestricted authority to suspend the proceedings indefinitely without fixing a subsequent date of hearing.

7. The expression sine die signifies an adjournment without fixing a date for the resumption of proceedings. Such an order, particularly when passed in a pending Sessions trial, has the effect of placing the entire prosecution in a state of indefinite suspension. It cannot be reconciled with the statutory scheme of Section 344, Cr.P.C., which contemplates adjournments from time to time for reasonable periods and not the indefinite postponement of proceedings. The Supreme Court of Pakistan [ ] strongly disapproved of a criminal reference having been kept adjourned sine die for years without any plausible reason, treating such indefinite postponement as an abuse of the process of law which keeps the accused under a perpetual cloud. The same principle is reflected in Rule 4-A, Chapter 1, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts) of the Rules and Orders of the Lahore High Court, which provides that it is not a reasonable cause for postponement under Section 344, Cr.P.C., except for a short [ ] National Accountability Bureau (NAB) through Chairman v. Messrs Hudaibya Paper Mills Limited and others (PLD 2018 SC 296)

period, that there are other accused in the case for whose arrest the Court considers it desirable to wait so that all the accused may be put on trial together, as every accused has a right to have the evidence against him recorded as early as possible. Recently, in Muhammad Khaliq’s Case [ ], this Court, dealing with the powers of a Court of Sessions in respect of an absconding accused, set aside an order of sine die adjournment, observing that the continuation of proceedings against the available accused persons would serve the ends of justice, while the evidence of the prosecution witnesses could be preserved and later used in accordance with Article 47 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984, subject to fulfilment of the statutory requirements. Thus, the mere fact that the principal accused is absconding does not, by itself, furnish lawful authority to the learned trial Court to suspend the entire trial for an indefinite period, particularly when the petitioner and the other available accused persons are appearing before the Court and are ready to face the proceedings.

8. It is also pertinent to observe that the absence of a coaccused does not necessarily render the continuation of proceedings against the remaining accused persons legally impermissible. The Code itself provides a mechanism to deal with an absconding accused. Section 512, Cr.P.C. enables the competent Court, subject to the satisfaction of the statutory conditions and compliance with Sections 87 and 88, Cr.P.C., to record the evidence of the prosecution witnesses in the absence of an accused who has absconded and of whose immediate arrest there is no prospect. The applicability of this mechanism, in backdrop of the question under consideration, was dilated upon by the august Supreme Court [ ] Muhammad Khaliq v. The State (2025 LHC 6151)

in Mohammad Saddique’s case [ ] wherein the Court has explained that, when an accused is absconding, the trial Court has to issue proclamation and attachment under Sections 87 and 88, Cr.P.C., and that, once the abscondence is established and proved on the record, the trial Court may proceed under Section 512, Cr.P.C. and record the evidence of the witnesses, which may later be used against the accused in the circumstances provided in Section 512(1), Cr.P.C. The object of this provision is to preserve the available evidence so that it is not lost on account of the passage of time or the subsequent unavailability of witnesses. In Muhammad Umair’s case [ ], a Division Bench of this Court held that the purpose of Section 512, Cr.P.C. is merely to preserve the evidence of a witness for an eventuality where such witness may not be alive at the time of the appearance of the accused, may have become incapable of giving evidence, or whose attendance cannot be procured without delay, expense or inconvenience.

Furthermore, Article 47 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 provides for the relevancy, in a subsequent judicial proceeding, of evidence given by a witness in an earlier judicial proceeding, subject to the conditions stipulated therein, including the requirements that the adverse party in the first proceeding had the right and opportunity to cross-examine the witness and that the questions in issue were substantially the same in both proceedings. Thus, the law itself provides safeguards for the preservation of evidence and does not contemplate that the rights of the available accused persons should remain suspended indefinitely on account of the abscondence of another accused. It is, however, clarified that the availability of [ ] Muhammad Saddique v. The State (2018 SCMR 71)

[ ] Muhammad Umair v. The State and another (2024 PCrLJ 183) Section 512, Cr.P.C. neither dispenses with the mandatory requirements of that provision nor authorises the recording of a conviction against an absconding accused in his absence. The learned trial Court shall exercise such jurisdiction strictly in accordance with law. The question whether the remaining accused can be tried independently, or whether any particular evidence necessitates a joint trial, has to be examined in the light of the facts of the case and the applicable provisions of law; it cannot, in any event, justify an indefinite suspension of the entire proceedings.

9. In the present case, the impugned order reflects that the proceedings were adjourned sine die solely because the principal accused, Arsalan alias Chochi Shah, was absconding. No specific impediment has been identified in the impugned order demonstrating that the trial against the petitioner and the other available accused persons could not proceed independently in accordance with the applicable provisions of law. A mere apprehension that separate proceedings might result in some inconvenience, or that the principal accused may subsequently be arrested, is not by itself sufficient to deprive the petitioner of his right to have the allegations against him determined through a regular trial. It is also significant that the petitioner is not seeking any determination of his innocence at this stage; rather, his grievance is confined to the indefinite suspension of the criminal proceedings. The petitioner has a legitimate interest in having the allegations against him adjudicated without unreasonable delay. The pendency of criminal proceedings, particularly where no date for their resumption has been fixed, results in an indefinite continuation of uncertainty and prejudice to the accused. Such a course is inconsistent with the spirit of Article 10-A of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973, which guarantees the right to a fair trial and due process. A speedy trial is the fundamental right of an accused, that the Code provides a methodology and scheme for speedy trial in recognition of that right, and that any unreasonable or shocking delay in the conclusion of a trial amounts to a denial of justice [ ]. The delay in the conclusion of a criminal trial is antithetic to the very concept of a "fair trial" and "due process" guaranteed by Article 10A of the Constitution [ ].

The learned trial Court, while exercising jurisdiction under Section 344, Cr.P.C., was required to examine whether any reasonable cause existed for a temporary adjournment and, if so, to determine a reasonable period for that purpose. Instead, by adjourning the proceedings sine die till the arrest of the principal accused, the learned trial Court has effectively suspended the trial without any ascertainable time limit. Such an exercise of jurisdiction is not sanctioned by the statutory framework and is contrary to the law laid down in the judgments referred to above.

10. For what has been discussed above, this Court is of the considered view that the impugned order suffers from material illegality and irregularity, resulting in an improper exercise of jurisdiction. The learned trial Court has failed to appreciate the distinction between a reasonable adjournment under Section 344, Cr.P.C. and an indefinite suspension of proceedings, which is not contemplated by the law governing Sessions trials. The impugned order, therefore, cannot be sustained. Consequently, the instant criminal revision petition is allowed. The impugned order dated 08.09.2025 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Mandi Bahauddin, is hereby set aside, and the learned trial Court is directed to proceed with the trial against the petitioner and [ ] Imtiaz Ahmed v. The State through Special Prosecutor, ANF (2017 S C M R 1194) [ ] Chairman NAB through P.G. Accountability v. Nasar Ullah and others (PLD 2022 SC 497)
the other available accused persons in accordance with law, without being influenced by the abscondence of the principal accused.
(Khalid Ibn-i-Aziz)
